accuracy.evidence: Checked against DfE Development Matters (2021) birth to three, Understanding the World ('explore materials with different properties', 'explore natural materials, indoors and outside') and the physics of wet granular matter (Hornbaker et al. 1997, Nature, 'What keeps sandcastles standing?'): dry grains flow and settle into a low cone, a little water forms liquid bridges that bind grains, and too much water makes sand runny again, which the adult text states. p2, p3, m5 and m7 give whole positive answers at every range corner (m7 min is 3-2=1).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the toddler ideas seen in sand-tray play: any sand makes a castle (step 1 prediction 'Yes, it stands up', challenge 'stands'), water makes sand fall apart (step 3 prediction 'No, the water makes it fall', m3 and challenge 'apart'), and a full cup can still take more (step 4 prediction, p4, challenge 'fits' and 'grow'); the spill animation in the cups step answers a pour into a full cup.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsand is the only lab about the changing behaviour of one material with water: dry sand pours and slumps to a heap, the same sand watered goes darker and holds a bucket shape as a castle, and water fills cups to full. flagwarm, flagsolid, flagtwist and flagair cover heat, solids, shape change by force and air; none model wet versus dry granular sand. The 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child scoops dry sand and sees it pour in, tips it out and watches it slump, then waters the sand and sees it darken, and tips the same bucket to get a standing castle, so the cause (water) is the only change between the two tips. The cups step makes full and empty concrete: each tap adds half a cup and a pour into a full cup spills. Each idea is shown before the line of text names it.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options taken from how toddlers talk at the sand tray: 'Will dry sand make a castle?' (Yes, it stands up), 'Will wet sand make a castle?' (No, the water makes it fall) and 'A cup is full. Can more water go in?' (Yes, lots more). The lab then shows the result straight after, so the child sees their guess tested.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with rotated answer order and 12 m= messages, one per wrong pick (dry, none, wetpour, castle, stands, bigger, fits, grow, fly, apart, white, same), each saying what really happens, for example 'The cup stays the same size. The extra water spills out.' Feedback is read out through an aria-live status line.

readability.evidence: Kid text is 4 short paragraphs of 3 to 4 word sentences built from the topic's own target words wet, dry, pour, full and empty, measured by the validator under the family kid limit; lab prompts are one short line each for a parent to read aloud. Adult text names the EYFS area, explains liquid bridges in plain words and lists the mistakes.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph carries one idea: dry sand pours, water makes sand wet and dark, wet sand keeps a shape, full and spills; the adult side gives the curriculum link, the reason, the common mistakes and what the lab does. The content gate's filler patterns all passed and the family tip is a two-castle test you can do at any sandpit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 in light and dark themes show the bucket, heap, castle and the three cups fully on the canvas with labels readable; the young class gives big buttons ('Scoop sand', 'Tip the bucket', 'Pour in cup 1-3'), and the sand colours are fixed earthy tones so wet sand reads darker in both themes. The walk gate passed all 5 tasks on phone and desktop.

accessibility.evidence: axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) ran clean in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13. The canvas aria-label updates with each action (e.g. 'Half full. Pour once more.'), every canvas tap has a matching labelled button, the cup buttons say whether each cup is empty, half full or full, and Challenge answers are real buttons in a labelled group.
